concept.body: Angle-name decoder: three letters, and the MIDDLE one is the vertex — the corner where the two rays meet. ∠XYZ and ∠ZYX are the same angle (vertex Y); moving a different letter to the middle names a different angle entirely.

explanationVariants: ∠PQR has middle letter Q, so its vertex is Q.
Trace the path P → Q → R: the corner is turned at Q.

options.label: P
options.feedback: P is an outer letter — it marks a point on one ray, not the corner.

options.label: Q
options.feedback: Middle letter = vertex. The rays run from Q through P and through R.

options.label: R
options.feedback: R is the other outer letter — out on a ray, not at the meeting point.

steps.body: Now build. A **segment AB** is the part of line AB between A and B, endpoints included. A **ray AB** starts at A and runs forever through B — the ENDPOINT is written first. An **angle** is two rays sharing an endpoint (the **vertex**). A **circle** is the set of ALL points at one fixed distance (the radius) from one fixed point (the center).
Match each term to its precise definition.

widget.prompt: Connect each term with its precise definition.

right.label: part of a line between two endpoints
part of a line with one endpoint, running forever one way
two rays that share an endpoint
all points at a fixed distance from a fixed point

pairErrors.feedback: A segment stops at BOTH ends. A ray has just one endpoint and never stops on the other side.
"Forever one way" is the ray's half-open signature — a segment is trapped between two endpoints.
Two rays make a corner, not a curve. The circle is a SET of points picked out by distance.

widget.missFeedback: Each definition names its building blocks: count the endpoints and directions to tell segment from ray.
widget.successFeedback: Four precise definitions, all built from point, line, and distance.

explanationVariants: The circle is the set of ALL points at distance r from the center — the boundary curve only. The center itself is NOT on the circle (its distance is 0, not r).
Precise definitions classify every point in or out: distance exactly r → on the circle; anything else (including inside points) → not.

widget.prompt: Using the precise definition, which points make up circle with center O and radius 5?

options.label: Every point at distance exactly 5 from O
options.feedback: The definition is a distance test: pass at exactly 5, you're on the circle; anything else, you're not.

options.label: Every point at distance 5 or less from O
options.feedback: Distance ≤ 5 describes the filled DISK. The circle is only the boundary — the points at exactly 5.

options.label: Every point inside the round shape, plus O
options.feedback: Interior points are closer than 5, so they fail the distance test — and O itself sits at distance 0.

options.label: The points where the circle crosses a line through O
options.feedback: That's just two points of it. The circle is ALL points at distance 5 — infinitely many, all the way around.

steps.body: Angle naming: **the vertex letter goes in the middle**. The angle with vertex Y made by rays YX and YZ is ∠XYZ or ∠ZYX — never ∠YXZ. When only one angle sits at a vertex, the single letter ∠Y is enough; when several share the vertex, three letters keep them apart.

hotspots.label: X
hotspots.feedback: X is on one RAY of the angle. The vertex is where the two rays meet — read the middle letter of ∠XYZ.

hotspots.label: Z
hotspots.feedback: Z is out on the other ray. The middle letter of the name — Y — marks the meeting point of the two rays.

widget.missFeedback: The middle letter of a three-letter angle name always marks the corner where the rays meet.
widget.successFeedback: Y — the middle letter is always the vertex.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents gf notation.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for gf notation must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines gf notation.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: The vertex is always the MIDDLE letter: in ∠STU the vertex is T.
Reading ∠STU as a path — from S, turn the corner at T, head to U — the turn happens at T, so T is the vertex.

widget.prompt: Which angle name has its vertex at T?

options.label: ∠STU
options.feedback: Middle letter T = vertex T. The rays run from T through S and through U.

options.label: ∠TSU
options.feedback: Here the middle letter is S — this angle's vertex is S, with T just a point on one ray.

options.label: ∠SUT
options.feedback: Middle letter U puts the vertex at U. T rides along a ray instead of sitting at the corner.

options.label: ∠UST
options.feedback: The middle letter is S again — same vertex-S angle as ∠TSU, just read from the other side.

steps.body: Ray order is strict: **ray FG starts at F**; ray GF starts at G — different objects, opposite tails. But two ray names CAN mean the same ray: if A, B, C sit on a line in that order, ray AB and ray AC both start at A and run the same way — same endpoint, same direction, same ray.

widget.prompt: Points A, B, C lie on a line in that order. Sort each ray by whether it is THE SAME as ray AB.

items.label: ray AC
items.feedback: Ray AC starts at A and runs through B on its way to C — same endpoint, same direction as ray AB.

items.label: ray BA
items.feedback: Ray BA starts at B and runs BACKWARD through A — opposite direction, and a different endpoint too.

items.label: ray BC
items.feedback: Ray BC points the same way but starts at B, so it's missing the piece from A to B. Same direction isn't enough — the endpoint must match.

items.label: ray CA
items.feedback: Ray CA starts at C and runs toward A — the reverse direction entirely.

widget.missFeedback: Two ray names match only when BOTH the starting endpoint and the direction agree.
widget.successFeedback: Same endpoint + same direction = same ray. Ray AC is ray AB wearing a different name.

hints: List what a valid name needs: which letter must sit in the middle?
The vertex is B, so the middle letter must be B — that eliminates some options instantly.
The outer letters must come from DIFFERENT rays, one from each side of the angle.
explanationVariants: A valid name puts the vertex B in the middle and takes one point from EACH ray: ∠ABD works. ∠ABС-style names fail when both outer letters ride the same ray.
Test each name: middle letter = B? outer letters on different rays? ∠DBA passes both tests — it's ∠ABD read backward.

widget.prompt: ∠ABD has vertex B; point C lies on ray BD beyond D. Which is a VALID alternate name for ∠ABD?

options.label: ∠ABC
options.feedback: C rides the same ray as D (ray BD extended through C is still ray BC = ray BD), so ∠ABC names the very same opening at vertex B.

options.label: ∠BAD
options.feedback: The middle letter here is A — that names an angle with vertex A, a different corner altogether.

options.label: ∠ADB
options.feedback: Middle letter D puts the vertex at D. Same three letters, wrong one in the middle.

options.label: ∠DBC
options.feedback: D and C sit on the SAME ray from B, so these two "sides" collapse into one ray — no opening, no angle.

takeaways: Segment = two endpoints; ray = one endpoint, one direction (endpoint written FIRST).
A circle is a distance test: all points at exactly r from the center.
Angle names put the vertex in the middle; outer letters come one from each ray.
